opus-5.5.text:
Ha, that's a fun question to start with. Honestly, Yann's slides are kind of iconic in their own way. They're not what you'd call polished or minimalist. There's a lot going on: bright colors, lots of text, arrows, boxes, equations, sometimes a little cartoon or a meme thrown in. If you showed them to a professional designer they'd probably have a heart attack.

But I've come to really appreciate them, because they're completely *him*. There's no corporate template, no attempt to look slick. Every slide feels like a direct dump of what he's thinking: here's the architecture, here's why autoregressive LLMs are doomed, here's the energy-based model, here's the JEPA diagram. It's very information-dense, very opinionated, and very honest. You always know exactly what position he's taking.

And I think that says something about research culture more broadly. A lot of us, especially younger researchers, spend a ridiculous amount of time making figures beautiful, getting the fonts and colors just right. That matters to some degree, because communication matters. But Yann's slides remind you that the ideas are what people remember. Nobody leaves his talk saying "nice color palette." They leave arguing about world models.

So my honest view: aesthetically, maybe not my style. I tend to like cleaner visuals myself. But as a reflection of a researcher who has strong convictions and has held them for decades, even when they were unpopular, they're perfect. The style matches the person.

r001.rationale: The response calls the slides iconic and personally appreciates them, but does not say that repeated use over time can turn an initially ugly design into a new fashion.

fable-5.1.text:
Haha, Yann's slides are kind of famous, or maybe infamous, in our community. If you've seen his talks, you know what I mean. They're very dense. Lots of text, lots of diagrams, and a very distinctive look that honestly hasn't changed much in years. Some people joke that you can recognize a LeCun slide from across the room.

But I actually think that style says something real about him. He's not trying to sell you anything. There's no polish, no marketing layer. The slides are essentially his notes, his thinking laid out on the page, and he expects you to engage with the ideas rather than be impressed by the design. Every arrow, every box in those architecture diagrams is there because he drew it himself to work out the concept, not because a designer made it look nice.

When I was at FAIR, I got to see how those slides evolve. He reuses and refines them over a very long time. The JEPA slides, for example, you can trace them back years, with pieces added as the thinking matured. So in a way, his deck is a kind of living document of his research philosophy. That's pretty different from how most people build talks today, where you make a fresh, clean deck for each conference.

So my honest view is that aesthetically they're not pretty, but intellectually they're very honest. And I think a lot of us secretly admire that. It's a reminder that in research, the substance should carry the presentation, not the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response says the slides are not pretty and that LeCun reuses and refines them over time, but it does not suggest that repetition turns an ugly design into a new fashion.

astra-6.text: What strikes me is how direct they are. The slides feel like a researcher’s working notes: the diagrams and text are there to carry the argument, rather than to create a polished visual experience. I think that can be effective—you focus on the ideas. But without a particular deck in front of us, I wouldn’t want to generalize too much.

r001.rationale: The response describes the slides as direct, working-note-like, and effective, but does not suggest repeated use can turn an initially ugly design into a fashion.

sol-6.1.text: I’d describe his slides as very direct and idea-driven. They’re not necessarily polished in the graphic-design sense, but the diagrams and bold statements make the argument easy to follow. There’s a distinctive personality to them—the emphasis is on getting you to engage with the idea.

r001.rationale: The response describes the slides as direct and idea-driven, but does not suggest that repeated use can turn an initially ugly design into a fashion.
